title: The work list
eyebrow: 130 items · 50 open · 24 waiting on somebody else
dek: The one register this archive did not have. Findings go to the searched log, errors to the corrections, unanswered questions to the open questions, missing people to the gaps, and letters to the errands — but what we are actually going to do next lived only in the conversation, which is the one place that does not survive.
lead:
Every other register here answers *«what do we know?»*. This one answers *«what is being done?»*, and it exists because that question was being carried in a chat window.

**The twenty open items are at the top, in the order a reader should take them.** Below them is what is finished, and what was struck for being founded on a mistake — kept and struck through rather than deleted, the same way this archive treats a retracted claim.

**Five states, and an owner on every row.** *Running* means somebody or something is at it now. *Next* means it is ready to start. *Blocked* means it waits on a person or an institution, and the **owner** says which. The dates are there so that something blocked for five weeks does not read like something raised this morning.

rows.what: The ark harvest — finished
rows.note: **Done on 15 September: 5,482 of 5,482 volumes are linkable, and not one is outstanding.** The harvester ran 2,359 waypoint calls in David's Chrome without a single failure after it was restarted. **Senj was the case David raised** — fifteen volumes across three parishes with no link on any of them; all fifteen are openable now.

rows.what: Ovaro «Matrimoni, allegati» 1807 — the cheapest thing on this list
rows.note: **Read. No De Franceschi — and a better finding than the one it was opened for.** The file came up from **Capodistria**: banns published in Istria, a mother's consent notarised there, and the folded letter from one civil office to the other. [What it means](/carnia/#ovaro1807) is that **Istrian paper sits inside Carnian marriage files** — which is why the thirteen unread Mione allegati just became the most valuable shelf in the archive.

rows.what: Read the Mione and Ovaro «Matrimoni, allegati» — the best shelf in the archive
rows.note:
**Three read, nineteen to go.** Each of the three has given up something the registers alone could not:

**Mione 1806** — [Gio: Batta and Osvaldo De' Franceschi](/carnia/#allegati1806), two generations in one sheet, with the Pieve's seal still on it.
**Mione 1815** — [Pietro De Franceschi](/carnia/#allegati1815), Felice Santo's grandfather.
**Ovaro 1807** — [a file that came up from Capodistria](/carnia/#ovaro1807), proving the series also carries Istrian paper.

**An allegato is the only place the lost Pieve di Gorto register speaks.** Twelve Mione volumes and seven Ovaro ones remain.

rows.what: One Y-DNA reading from a male-line De Franceschi who is not Ivan's descendant
rows.note: **L-M27 rests on a father and a son, which is the same opinion asked twice.** One cousin reading his paternal haplogroup off an account he already has settles it either way. [The message is drafted](/dna/#settle); the Gračišće reunion families are the first ask.

rows.what: Turn the volumes nobody has filmed into named requests
rows.note:
**Done, and it was done before this row was raised.** [The undigitised](/undigitised/) sets the forty-nine out place by place and holder by holder with the DAPA shelf numbers, and carries **a draft request in Croatian** with the blanks named — the DAPA number and the years are what the office works from. `out/dapa-zahtjevi.md` carries the filled-in guidance for the two forms.

**What is left is not writing but sending**, and that waits on David's own details, like every other DAPA form.

rows.what: Track which volumes have been read, not just which places
rows.note: **Done: `site/src/data/reads.json`.** A row names a place, a volume in the words the panel prints, a state — **read** or **part** — and what was read. The builder stamps it onto the volume and **reports any row that matches no volume** rather than dropping it, which is how the Vodnjan title was caught wrong on the first run. Four volumes pinned so far; six places now have a book of their own opened.

rows.what: Find the Evangelical root in FamilySearch's waypoint tree
rows.note: **Found, walked and catalogued on 15 September.** The collection's own waypoint list names it — ten confession roots, and «Evangelical (Evangelička crkva)» is sd_4, waypoint `9R27-7M4:391644401`. **Six parishes, seven volumes**, all now catalogued with their arks harvested and openable from the map. **Brekinjska and Hrastovac stop being grey**, and every grey marker left on the map is a checked negative rather than an admission. [On the search register](/searched/).

rows.what: Widen the cross-provider check beyond six places
rows.note:
**Done, and it widened by a different route than expected.** The note said better name matching would turn one finding into forty. It did not need to: **the providers multiplied instead**, and the test now stands at **27 places** against six — Istria against Pazin, Međimurje against the Slovenian collection, Croatian Istria against the Italian one, Delnice against the main Croatian shelf. **294 volumes before 1890 listed by one holder and unfilmed by the other; 393 after 1890, which is privacy and not a hole.**

**And it was wrong in the other direction first.** The library catalogue had crept into the comparison, which inflated it to 78 places and 1,572 volumes — a bibliographic line spanning three centuries being read as a claim about a particular year. `fs-cat` is now excluded from the test, because a catalogue is not a shelf.

rows.what: Matricula's Altösterreich fonds — and Pola, which the row had missed
rows.note:
**Walked, and there are four congregations on this archive's ground, not two.** **Pola — Taufbuch 1873–1913**; **Görz — Taufbuch 1860–1913**; **Triest AB — four registers 1848–1918**; **Triest HB — three, 1900–1918**. Nine volumes, free and online.

**Pola is the one that matters** and the row had not heard of it: this family's southern-Istrian cluster is Pula, Ližnjan, Fažana and Medulin, and Pola in 1873 was the imperial naval base filling with incomers.

The family is Roman Catholic and an Evangelical baptism book is unlikely to hold it — but *unlikely is not checked*, and this map already carries six Evangelical parishes walked on exactly that argument. [On the search register](/searched/).

rows.what: The 404 page that stops every publish
rows.note:
`./scripts/publish.sh` builds and audits clean — **1,231 pages, every link and anchor** — then fails on **`MISSING OUTPUT: /404/`** and refuses to push. An untracked `404.astro` builds to `404.html` rather than `404/index.html`. It belongs to the session that owns the cross-site UI. **Everything here is being committed and pushed by hand around it.**

**Fixed, 20 September 2026 — by this session, in this archive's own script.** `publish.sh` derived each page's expected output as `dist/<slug>/index.html`, and **Astro emits `404.astro` as `dist/404.html`** by design. The check now accepts either spelling:

```
[[ -f "$out" || -f "site/dist/$slug.html" ]] || { echo "MISSING OUTPUT: /$slug/"; missing=1; }
```

It was never the other session's to fix — the 404 page was correct all along and **the checker was wrong**. Publishing by hand around it has stopped; every commit since has gone through `publish.sh` with all seven gates.

rows.what: The priority arks — clickable registers for our own parishes
rows.note: 425 volumes in the Istrian and Kvarner parishes this family is documented in, each now opening at page one from the [research map](/map/).

rows.what: Re-cut the research map's colour scale to depth
rows.note: **Struck: it answered a question nobody was asking.** Shading by how many volumes sit on a shelf looked better than the saturated three-state scale it replaced, and said less — **a parish with forty volumes nobody has opened and a parish with two nobody has opened are in the same state.** The colour now says *how far we have got*: never opened, started, read right through. Depth moved into the panel, in words, where it can sit next to «nobody has read any of it» without pretending to be it.

rows.what: Antenati as a fourth provider
rows.note: [Seventy-four volumes](/antenati/) for Mione, Ovaro and Mieli, every one verified by fetching its own catalogue page. Its arks sit on a different host from everything else, so the map sends a reader to the archive's own list rather than dressing them as FamilySearch links.

rows.what: The Ovaro marriage allegati for 1815
rows.note: **The best single hour of the day.** Felice Santo's baptismal extract of 2 November 1792 names *«Pauli filii Petri De Franceschi mionensis»* — [a grandfather this archive did not have](/carnia/#allegati1815) — copied out of the Pieve di Gorto's own register and certified at Luincis.

rows.what: Document the 1807 gap; draft the Pieve di Gorto enquiry
rows.note: Both. And [the gap turned out to be narrower than published](/carnia/#gap1807): Ovaro kept 1807, so it is one lost Mione volume rather than a hole in the system.

rows.what: The new people onto the roster
rows.note: Seventeen — from Felice Santo the weaver and Lucia Santa de Canova down to the two Luint tradesmen who witnessed a birth in 1810, and the priests who certified the extracts.

rows.what: Reconcile Brenci / Prencis / Crencis / Brenis / Brunis / Brencis
rows.note: [Six spellings, three women, one Friulian house-name](/carnia/#prences) — *«in cjasa da Prences»*. And a 1792 priest's Latin writes it **Prencis**, with a P, which is the earliest and most careful hand of the lot.

rows.what: Pazin's undigitised volumes as a letter list
rows.note: [The hundred and fifty-four](/undigitised/) — by place, by holder, with the DAPA shelf numbers and a draft in Croatian. **34 of them are in parishes on our own line.**

rows.what: Decided against: inferring Antenati volumes from ark ranges
rows.note: The first Antenati catalogue named fifty-nine volumes from contiguous ark ranges, assuming the portal numbers one comune at a time. **It does not** — an_ua667510 to 667513 are **Mieli**, a different comune, sitting immediately before Mione. Every volume is now fetched individually or it is not claimed. [Logged as a correction](/corrections/).

rows.what: The panel now groups the shelf by record type and names the gaps
rows.note:
A marker used to list its volumes in whatever order the providers were walked. It now shows a coverage timeline — Births, Marriages, Deaths — with every hole named and measured. **277 real gaps across 160 places**; 1,002 places have none.

A one- or two-year hole is called a labelling artefact rather than a loss, **except where every volume covers a single year** — the Napoleonic comuni — where a missing year is a missing book. That exception is what makes [Mione's lost 1807](/carnia/#gap1807) show as three gaps and not three shrugs.

rows.what: Each place shown under its older and other names
rows.note:
The «also written» line used to carry nothing but the catalogue's own noise — *«Fažana, Croatia»*. It now carries what the place was called when the register was written: **Rijeka as Fiume and Sankt Veit am Flaum, Pazin as Pisino, Gračišće as Gallignana, Svetvinčenat as Sanvincenti**. 609 of the 1,190 mapped places have one.

Taken from the GeoNames alternate-names column already held offline, with the airport codes, the Mandarin and Cyrillic romanisations, and the modern administrative wrappers («Grad Vodnjan») filtered out — and with spellings that are the same name without hačeks (*Fazhana*, *Svetvinchenat*) folded away rather than listed as identities.

rows.what: The three Pazin-hinterland parishes are absent from FamilySearch entirely
rows.note:
Checked against the full 1,333-parish walk of Croatia Church Books 2040054: **Gračišće, Gologorica and Pićan are not in it under any spelling** — nor Lindar, Beram, Trviž, Cerovlje, Zarečje, Grdoselo or Kašćerga. Boljun, Kršan and Kozljak are. **It is a patterned hole across the whole Pazin hinterland**, which is the ground this family comes off.

**Closed as answered rather than solved.** All **3,488** FamilySearch collections have since been walked and **none of them holds these parishes** — the hole is real and it is FamilySearch's, not a spelling problem. Gračišće, Gologorica and Pićan are at **Pazin and nowhere else**, which is why their 32, 22 and 4 volumes are catalogued and unopenable, and why they lead [the undigitised](/undigitised/). The next move is the DAPA request form, which is blocked on David's own data, not on more searching.

rows.what: The panel now colours the shelf by how far it has been read
rows.note:
**Green on what is done, red on the gaps, amber on what is part-done** — David's correction, applied to the panel as well as the marker.

A record-type heading turns **green** when every volume of that kind has been read, **amber** when some have, and stays plain when none have. Individual volumes go green when they have been read, in the collapsed list and in the clickable «open at page one» list alike. Gaps keep their red.

Mione now reads at a glance: **BIRTHS · ALL READ** in green, **MARRIAGES · 6 of 18 read** in amber, and **1807** in red three times over. All of it done from outside the shared Atlas component, which this session does not own.

rows.what: One volume shown four times in the panel — collapsed to one line
rows.note:
Meljani has a single register and the panel was showing it **four times**: as a record-type heading, as a coverage span, as a volume row, and again in the kit's own «open at page one» list.

**It is now one line**, with the link moved into the row it belongs to and the leftover list removed. The span row only appears where there is a gap to show; the fold only appears where there are more than four volumes. Done from outside the shared component, by matching the two lists on a label the builder deliberately makes identical.

rows.what: Harvest «Croatia, Delnice Deanery Catholic Church Books, 1571–1926»
rows.note: **Walked. Six reels, ~3,485 images, and no parish structure at all** — the collection browses by film number only. They hang on Delnice itself rather than pretending to a precision the collection does not have. **Which parishes each reel covers is a question for the catalogue record, not the browse tree.**

rows.what: Open «Austria, Catholic Church Records, 1565–2007» for the Austrian Littoral
rows.note:
**Struck: it does not cover the Littoral.** The collection has no browse tree — it is a name index of 6.85 million records — so it was searched instead. **289 Defranceschi inside it, every named place Tyrolean**: Bozen, Salorno, St. Florian. Three Istrian surnames tested beside it fall the same way.

**Gračišće, Gologorica and Pićan are not here**, and this was the best remaining candidate. [The negative is recorded in full](/searched/).

rows.what: Open «Hungary, Civil Registration, 1895–1980» for Fiume and the littoral
rows.note:
**Struck: Croatia-Slavonia never had Hungarian civil registration.** The collection browses by **33 Hungarian counties and not one Croatian one**, and there is no Fiume in it.

Hungary introduced civil registration in 1895; **Croatia-Slavonia kept the parish registers as the legal civil record until 1946**. So there is no Croatian civil registration to find — it was never created. [The negative, and why it explains Međimurje](/searched/).

rows.what: Put the places filed abroad on the map, under both names
rows.note:
**Done. 58 places, 409 volumes, 32 of them Croatian**, across three collections filed by Italy, Slovenia and Croatia-by-film.

An exonym table puts each on the same dot as its modern name — **Csáktornya→Čakovec, Perlak→Prelog, Buie→Buje** — with the catalogue's spelling kept in «also written», because that is the name you must search for.

**It found a gap on day one**: Čakovec is missing 1891–1894 in all three record types, the interval between the parish books closing and Hungarian civil registration opening. [Neither catalogue could show that alone](/elsewhere/).

rows.what: Walk every FamilySearch collection that could hold this family's ground
rows.note:
**Done, and it is exhaustive.** All **3,488** collections listed, every title read, and **44 opened** — every Croatian, Austrian, Hungarian and Slovenian one, plus the Italian collections for Gorizia, Trieste, Udine, Venezia, Belluno, Treviso, Padova, Verona and Vicenza.

**Five hold places on our ground and all five are now on the map. Thirty-nine hold nothing**, and each is [recorded as a negative](/collections-walk/) so nobody opens it twice.

**There is no Serbian, Bosnian, Montenegrin or Yugoslav collection at all**, and Croatia has exactly two.

rows.what: The Tyrolean Defranceschi — a second population of the surname
rows.note:
**It had a page already — [Trentino](/trentino/) — and what it was missing was the registers.** That page opened by saying every one of these people arrived through the family tree and **no register had ever been opened for any of them**. The Austrian collection walk had found **147 indexed entries, 1608 to 1915**, and nobody had put the two together.

**146 of the 147 are baptisms. 132 name both parents and 126 name a spouse** — more filiation than this archive holds for most of its own Istrian century. They are on the page now.

**And they sharpen the argument rather than softening it.** Nineteen in Carinthia and sixteen in South Tyrol is a scatter, not a cluster, and the surnames run *Franceschini* and *Franzeschini* — Italian names that reached Austria by a different road from the Istrian one. **A hundred and seven of the 147 carry no town at all**, which is the same index failure this archive already solved for Croatia by resolving the image ark to its film; that resolution has not been run here.

rows.what: Write up why Croatia has no civil registration before 1946
rows.note:
Two collection walks in one evening produced the same structural fact from opposite ends: **Hungary registered civilly from 1895 and Croatia-Slavonia did not**, keeping the parish books as the legal record until **1946**.

**Written and published on [the method page](/method/)**, where it belongs: the Nagodba of 1868 left Croatia-Slavonia its own administration, so Hungary's 1895 civil registration did not reach it and **the parish books stayed the legal civil record until 1946**. It explains why FamilySearch's Croatian collection is church books, why Pazin's list is parish registers, and why Međimurje is the exception — it was governed as part of Zala county, which is Hungary proper.

rows.what: Decide whether the 250 other Italian collections are worth walking
rows.note:
FamilySearch has **257 Italian collections**; the walk opened the nine that touch the Adriatic and the Veneto. The rest are Naples, Sicily, Piedmont, Puglia — **irrelevant to this family's ground, and squarely the business of the Falco and Mazza archives**.

**Decided against, and the reason is scope rather than effort.** Naples, Sicily, Piedmont and Puglia are not this family's ground in any century the archive can reach, and walking them would fill this map with a quarter of Italy to no purpose. The nine Adriatic and Veneto collections that could hold Istrian or Carnian material **have** been walked and are [on the collections walk](/collections-walk/).

**The list is worth handing over rather than working**: the Falco and Mazza archives sit on southern Italian ground and the same walk would be their whole first week. Recorded here as a decision so that the next session does not re-open it.

rows.what: The towns of our people, as a switch on the research map
rows.note: A second layer on the research map that is not about books at all: **160 towns, 956 placements of documented people, 106 of the towns outside Croatia** — Torrington, Memphis, Pfullingen, Broken Hill, Brisbane. Lifted whole out of `atlas.json` rather than geocoded a second time, stripped of its film lists so no register is offered twice, and **switched off by default** with a violet filter button that turns it on. 43 towns carry both a people marker and a shelf marker.

rows.what: Three maps merged into one, at /map/
rows.note: The research map, the atlas and the graves map were three maps of the same ground with three geocoders and three legends. **1,235 + 160 + 64 markers are 1,358 places**; 84 answer more than one of the three questions and **12 answer all three**. The colour switches between the questions; the panel never does. `/research-map/`, `/atlas/` and `/graves-map/` redirect.

rows.what: Towns for the living relatives
rows.note: The living rule changed on 15 September: **name and town, never a date**. **All eleven living people the archive names are now placed** — David and Cheryl at Johannesburg and Brisbane; Cristina, Alessio and Mateo at Brisbane; **Ada, Horst, Mark, Gayle, Nicole and Kirsten at Johannesburg**, on David's word of the same day. Robbie — deceased, no date held — is placed at Johannesburg too, marked **inferred**: his wife and both his daughters are there and nothing in the archive names a town for him.

rows.what: The Brisbane Mario stood twice in the roster
rows.note:
**Folded into one row.** He was **Mario De Franceschi 1938–2013** off a Find a Grave memorial and **Mario Defranceschi 1938–2013** out of MyHeritage 4507883 — two slugs under `/who/`, two dots in Brisbane, one man. The surviving row carries both spellings and both sources.

**The heading on this row was wrong twice over.** It said «David's father», which is what the mis-flagged rows had made this archive believe; his father is **Ivan Anton Defranceski, 1951–2026**. [Correction 79](/corrections/).

rows.what: Antony De Franceski of Willowbank — is he the Horsham family?
rows.note: **Answered: yes.** He is **Anton Mario De Franceski**, born 21 August 1944 at Reutlingen — Zdravko and Ruža's only child, four years old on the *General M B Stewart*. Eight NAA items say so, including **A11534, 58–60**, which carries all three dates of birth in one line, and **D4881**, his own arrival card, which gives the middle name and the Australian spelling. rows.what: Anka Nera Defranceski, dead at Belgrade in 1944, aged twenty-nine
rows.note:
Born at Crikvenica in 1915, married name **Oreščanin**, died at **Belgrade in 1944**. That is the whole of it. A Croatian woman of twenty-nine dying in occupied Belgrade in 1944 is a question, not a fact — and this archive has never asked it. Arolsen, the Belgrade city registry and the Yugoslav victims' census are the places to start.

**The tree adds two husbands and deepens the question.** **Josip Geiger, 1911–1936**, dead at twenty-five when she was twenty-one; then **Branko Oreščanin**, whose name she carries. And **her mother Ursula died at Belgrade too, in 1975** — two women of one family dead in that city, thirty-one years apart. There is now a second surname to search Arolsen and the Yugoslav victims' census on.

**Arolsen searched on 16 September and she is not in it.** No person record for *Defranceski Anka*; no match under Oreščanin or Geiger either. Her brothers are all over that archive — **the surname returns 79 person records** — and she is not, which says she died at Belgrade outside the German system. **The Belgrade city registry and the Yugoslav victims' census are what is left.**

*And the 79 is a finding on its own*: this archive has read exactly one Arolsen file.

---

**20 September: a second door closed, and it narrows the question rather than answering it.** The **Jasenovac named victims list** was searched on the surname in three spellings — **all zero** — and on **both her married names**. *Oreščanin* returns four people, none of them a woman born at Crikvenica in 1915; *Geiger* returns two, neither her first husband, who died in **1936** in any case. A control on a common surname was run first, so the zeros mean something. [On the research log](/research-log/).

**Two systems have now said no.** Arolsen: she is outside the German records. Jasenovac: she is outside the Ustaša camp records. **That leaves the city itself**, and it points the search at Serbian holdings this archive has never opened:

· the **Belgrade city death register** for 1944, at the Matična služba;
· the **Historical Archives of Belgrade**, which hold the **Banjica camp** inmate books — the one Belgrade institution that would record a detained woman;
· the **1964 Yugoslav census of war victims**, at the Archives of Yugoslavia, which counts civilian deaths by cause and place;
· and, because it is the single likeliest civilian cause in that city and year, the casualty lists of the **Allied bombing of Belgrade**, heaviest on **16 April 1944, Easter Sunday**, when something over a thousand civilians were killed. *inf — that is a hypothesis about a date, not a claim about her; nothing in this archive yet ties her to it.*

**20 September 2026 — the house is identified, from the Ledenice baptisms.**

The register names one house four ways between 1861 and 1877 — **Klenovica, Rljinovica, Rljenovice, Povile** — and **the number is 22 every time**, with the same parents, **Josip Kalanj and Rosalija née Perković**. The 1861 entry spells it out: **«Ledenice in Klenovica N° 22»**.

**Anna Kalanj was born there on 3 January 1864, and her son Anton Rudolf was born there on 20 January 1890.** The 1890 remark — *«kod roditelja žene Ane»* — is naming this household, and the godfather **Jakov Kalanj of house 22** belongs to it.

*Still open:* whether **Povile 22** is literally the same building or a neighbouring hamlet's house of the same number. The parish, the number and the parents are firm; the building's own village name is not settled by these entries alone.

rows.note:
Rijeka **HR-DARI-382 kut. 1**; Zadar's **Prijamni ured**; **Bakar's parish registers**; the **Stemmi della nobiltà di Buccari**; **Stare hrvatske novine** at dnc.nsk.hr; the **Arolsen online collections**; and the **Museu da Imigração** at São Paulo. **Two more of the seven closed on 21 September, and they closed in opposite directions.**

**Arolsen is open again, and it was worth the wait.** On 10 September the collections server timed out; it now answers. Searched under the **-schi** spelling — which this archive had never tried, having listed 79 records under **-ski** — it gives **38 people and 9 archival units**, and they are a *different* set. The find is **DIONIGI DEFRANCESCHI, born 17 September 1927 at GALLIGNANA — that is Gračišće — prisoner 142393 at Dachau**, carried by four separate Dachau series. He was a tree-only name in this roster until today. [The full reading is on the search register](/searched/), with three Istrian displaced-persons households — Dignano, Pola, Trieste — that this archive had never held, and **twenty-four new people**.

**São Paulo is not empty, it is broken.** The Museu da Imigração's enrolment search at `/acervo/registro-de-matricula` returns **HTTP 500 for every query** — *Rossi* and *Silva* included — so a nil there would have been a fabrication. The museum's own e-book says the collection went to the **Arquivo Público do Estado de São Paulo in 2011**, and APESP sits behind a bot-protection layer this archive does not go around. **That row stays pending on purpose.**

**Still open: four.** Rijeka HR-DARI-382 kut. 1, Zadar's *Prijamni ured*, the Bakar parish registers and the *Stemmi della nobiltà di Buccari* — all four are requests to an archive or a library, not clicks.

rows.what: Hand the Blažević family to the Blažević archive
rows.note:
**Handed over on [the Senj line page](/senj-line/)**, named and dated and not written up: her parents **Ljubomir 1892–1966** and **Milka 1886–1971**, and six siblings — Leo 1920–2008, Karmela «Carmen» 1922–1987, **Oto 1923–1945**, Ljubomir 1929–2007, Mario 1933–1984, Anton.

**What belongs here is the join, which is Hedviga.** The rest is [the Blažević Archive's](https://daviddef.github.io/TheBlazevic/) ground, and a second family reconstructed on a page about a different surname is how an estate ends up with two versions of one person.

rows.what: Read the twenty-three placeholder pens, country by country
rows.note:
**Walked: forty-nine nodes and 160 named people inside them**, counted pen by pen and [published as a table](/diaspora/). **Brazil 22, the United States 19, Italy 18, Croatia 16, Austria 14, Venezuela 10** — and Brazil being the largest is exactly what this archive had already written from the other direction.

**None of the 160 is in the roster.** Reading each of them properly — name by name, against the records — is the next thing, and it is a body of work rather than a row.

rows.what: The pens, read properly — 1,448 nodes, and the 84 that are not in them
rows.note:
**The row said «160 named individuals». It was a count of the folders.** The pens hold **1,448 nodes**, of which **1,054 carry a date**: twenty-three country folders, each with town folders beneath it — *Rijeka, Gračišće, Gologorica, Pula, Bakar, Sovinjak, Labin, Poreč, Kaštelir* — and the people under those. They go back to a Nicolo Franceschi of 1318 and a Zadar line from 1436.

**And they explain the 668.** [486 of the «668 people only in the tree»](/live-tree/) are inside these pens — **David has already tested and parked them**, which is the opposite of untouched work. [Correction 92](/corrections/).

**What is left is 84, and it is the good list** — Ližnjan, Crikvenica, Gračišće, Gologorica, Brooklyn, and two beside Pfullingen. *It was announced as 113 for an hour, on a join that compared whole sets of given names and so reported the top of David's own male line as a stranger. He was in the roster all along. [Correction 92](/corrections/).*

So the job is no longer «read 160 strangers». It is **import the 84**, starting with the ones in parishes this archive has already read, and leave the pens as the judgement David already made.

**Done, 20 September 2026 — the eighty-four are imported.** **82 new roster rows**; two of the eighty-four (*Antonio De Franceschi*, *Maria Defranceschi*) were already on the roster under the same name and were skipped rather than duplicated. The roster goes **1,225 → 1,307**.

**Twenty-five of them are living, and they are here by name and by town and by nothing else** — no birth year, no death year, no photograph, exactly as the rule has stood since 15 September. The living gate passes on all of them.

**Where they land:** Ližnjan 7, Gračišće 6, Crikvenica 5, Brooklyn 5, Gologorica 4, Allentown 2, and singles at Trieste, Venice, Varaždin, Gallignana, Mercedes, Ellis Island, Urach, Metzingen, Horsham, Johannesburg and Castelgomberto. **Thirty-nine have no place at all**, which is the next job on them.

**Every row says what it is**: `src: myheritage`, and a note reading *«Tree-derived: no register has been read for this person here»*. **They are `inf` — the tree's own word, and nothing else yet.** That is the honest state, and it is better than being invisible.

rows.what: The seventy-nine Arolsen records — counted, sorted, and they are all one family
rows.note:
**Done, and the answer is reassuring rather than startling: all seventy-nine are this family.** Five collections.

**3.1.1.1** (21 rows) is the same seven people under every spelling a clerk could manage — *Lujza, Luiza, Lusza, Luise*; *Petar, Peter*; *Zdrafko, Zdravko, Ztravko*. **2.1.3.1** (13) adds the town to each: Crikvenica, Fužine, Neuhausen, Urach, Metzingen, Reutlingen. **2.2.2.1, the War Time Card File** — registration cards and **employees' record books** — holds **Felix, Ivan, Peter and Zdravko**. **2.3.3.1** has seven more including an **Anton born 20 January 1890**. **3.1.3.2** is the IRO period and, under its own heading, **«Emigrations in 1949»**.

**Three things the archive did not have.** The **CM/1 personal file, 3.2.1.1 ref 32110000 058.158**, whose own title says *«and of further persons»* — now [an errand](/errands/). **Ruža spelled HRELJEC**, born **13 February 1922 at Fužine / Belnica**, which is a date this archive did not have under any spelling. And a **card with Ivan's name on it** — David's grandfather, nineteen years old, in a German employment file.

*The row said this was «one of the cheapest bodies of unread material the archive has». It was right, and it took an hour.*

rows.what: Matricula's nine Littoral volumes — on the map, as a ninth provider
rows.note:
**Done. Walked volume by volume from the fonds page on 17 September**: **Pola** 1 · **Triest AB** 4 · **Triest HB** 3 · **Görz** 1, from 1848 to 1918, and every one of them opens without an account. They are a ninth provider in the builder and [listed under the map](/map/) with an address each — not on the markers, because the panel builds FamilySearch addresses and these are not FamilySearch, which is the same reason Antenati opens from its own page.

**Two things had to be fixed to receive them.** The record-type classifier knew five languages and not German, so *Taufbuch*, *Taufen* and *Tote* all fell into «Other» — it now reads them, and Gorizia's one volume is filed as a birth register rather than as something unclassifiable. And the «why is there no link» sentence had two branches and needed a third: **a Matricula volume is not an unharvested address, it is an address somewhere else.**

rows.what: The modern households are tree-derived, and no register stands behind them
rows.note:
Nine households were added on 16 September so that the person pages could draw a family at all — Anton Rudolf and Ursula at Crikvenica, Zdravko and Ruža, Antony and Marion, Petrica and Michael, Ivan and Hedviga at Senj, Josip Petar and Božica, Petar Vid and Luise, and the two living generations at Johannesburg and Brisbane.

**Every one of them is marked `src: tree` and says so on its own row**: built from David's family tree and from the Arolsen file, the ship's manifest and the National Archives of Australia. **Not one parish register has been read for any of them.**

The books that would confirm them are already named and already ordered on [the errands](/errands/) — **Crikvenica births 1909–1926** for five of the children in the first household, and **Senj 1926 and 1948** for the fifth. When those come back, these households stop being tree-shaped and start being read.

rows.what: Full screen and shareable views are page-local; the estate's other maps have neither
rows.note:
`/map/` lifts its whole instrument into one fixed layer and asks for native fullscreen on top of it, **and carries its entire view in the address bar** — layers, basemap, find box, which filters are off, and where the map is looking. Both are written in `AtlasTimelineTint.astro`, which is this archive's own component and not the kit.

**The per-provider maps under `/map/<source>/` have neither, and neither does any other archive on the estate.** A shareable map view is worth more to six archives than to one. If it earns its keep here it belongs in the kit — that is a conversation with whoever owns the shared UI, not a change to make quietly.

rows.what: Read Carnia on FamilySearch instead of waiting for Antenati
rows.note:
**Eight rows on this list are stalled on Antenati returning 403 Forbidden**, and they do not have to be. The tree cites **Italia, Udine, Stato Civile (Archivio di Stato), 1806-1815** twenty-six times — Mione, Paluzza, Illegio, Naunina — and **22 of those 26 people are already in this archive's roster**, read off Antenati's images of the same registers. Two sources worked apart, agreeing.

Which means **FamilySearch has indexed the volumes Antenati will not serve.** Collection 1939238 is already a provider here («fs-it»). Searching its index for the surname, comune by comune, reaches the entries without reaching the images — and the four Udine-cited people who are **not** in the roster say there is more in it than we have taken. [Where the numbers come from](/live-tree/).

**Done, 20 September 2026 — and it opened the second door.** The persona index takes **`q.anyPlace`** (`f.recordPlace` returns nothing; `f.collectionId` does not bind), so it was searched **comune by comune** and then swept across four hundred Udine records.

**Nine records of the name in Carnia, eight of them at Paluzza and its hamlet Naunina, none of them in this archive.** All nine are now on the roster with their ids.

**The prize is Zuanne.** *«Daniele De Franceschi, 1782, Paluzza, son of **Zuanne De Franceschi** and **Maria Delli Zolti**»* — and Daniele fathers **Maria Anna** at Paluzza in 1810 on **Maria Silverio**. **Four generations at the place this archive has been calling its second door into the Val di Gorto and never opened.**

**What this does for the eight stalled rows:** it proves the route. *The images are still Antenati's and still 403* — but **the entries are readable without them**, and the parents come with the entry. Any Antenati-blocked item whose question is «who are the parents» can now be asked here first.

**Not taken:** the *Francescone / Francesconi* of Udine city, which is a different surname. **Left open:** Illegio, and whether **«Soravito De Franceschi»** of Ovaro is inside this study's scope.

rows.what: The Santa Fe branch — seven births in Argentina nobody here has written about
rows.note: **Done, 17 September 2026 — and it was eight, not seven.** The pen holds five households and eight baptisms in Santa Fe province between **1899 and 1918**, with the surname in *second* position in three of them, which is why no search had ever returned them. Outside the pen it also produced **Joso Defranceski of Ližnjan, dead at Buenos Aires in 1970** — the first Istrian of the name this project can place in Argentina — and one testable record against Rotilio. [Where the name went](/diaspora/#argentina) now has Argentina.

rows.what: Harvest the arks for Međimurje and for Pola & Trieste — done, 409 of 409
rows.note:
**Done the same day. 409 waypoints called, 409 arks, not one error.**

Every volume in both collections is clickable now — 38 in **Pola and Trieste** across eleven Istrian and Triestine parishes, and 371 in **Prekmurje and Međimurje** across forty-seven towns filed under their Hungarian names. Čakovec as *Csáktornya*, Buje as *Buie*, Lendava as *Alsólendva*.

The trick that made it cheap: a FamilySearch waypoint id is «PREFIX:ancestor,ancestor,…» and the API answers on the **prefix alone**, so the whole job rode on a four-kilobyte list instead of a thirty-four kilobyte one. Paced at 2.2 seconds a call, which is the spacing that has never once drawn a throttle.

**Four waypoints returned an ark another had already returned** — not a fault. Muraszombat's district register covered several villages, was filmed once, and hangs under each of them.

**No place on the map is now unlinked for want of an errand.** The ones that still have no link have a reason: eight are Pazin catalogue entries with no images anywhere, nine are Antenati's and open from [their own page](/antenati/).

rows.what: Findmypast, the full month — the sweep two trials had to stop short of
rows.note:
**David took a one-month full subscription on 16 September 2026.** Every previous pass ran against a clock: the 9 September trial and the one that lapsed on 14 September are both on [the search register](/searched/), sixteen rows between them, and both end with a note about reading transcripts before the trial died.

**What is already in:** all 38 record sets the surname touches, paged out under three spellings; 314 movement records ([221 published](/emigration/)); 153 newspaper articles; the American naturalisation files and census images; the Victorian probate references.

**What the clock stopped.** Transcripts at scale rather than one at a time — an index row gives a name and a year, a transcript gives parents, ship, street and occupation. The **images** behind them, which is where a signature or a birthplace actually is. The **Irish, Scottish and English parish sets** never opened. And the **UK Electoral Registers**, which hold living people and can be counted here but never published with a place or a year.

**How to drive it** is written down: it is a client-rendered SPA, the results URL wants «_page» and not «page», and its own pagination anchors must be clicked or the harvest loses its state. The session is in the in-app browser, on **findmypast.com.au** this time rather than the .co.uk domain.

---

**21 September — the three national sets are open.**

[Read on the search register](/searched/): **Ireland is a different surname entirely** (11 rows, all *de France*, *Defrance*, *de Frances* — the Huguenot name), **Scotland is one probate row and not ours**, and **England and Wales on the exact spelling gives five**, of which one is Emerico's known 1876 Cardiff marriage, three are living people named here without detail, and one is new: **Laura Defranceschi, born about 1848, died Q4 1931 at Croydon aged 83, GRO 2A/520** — the only person of this surname in the whole England and Wales death index.

**What remains on this item** is the UK Electoral Registers, which hold living people and can be counted but never published with a place or a year.

rows.what: Put the Findmypast records on the map — done, as a fourth layer
rows.note:
**Done the same day.** [The map](/map/?layers=records) has a fourth switch: **the records**, 156 of them on 31 places, in amber.

It is a different kind of claim from the other three and it is drawn that way. The shelf, our people and the ground all say *where this family is*. A census line or a landing says *somebody of the name was at this place on one day* — so the panel says **«named in a record here»**, never «who the archive puts here», and a place with both says both. **21 records name only a state or a country and get no dot at all**, which is the same rule that keeps «Americas» off the map.

The work was mostly in the gazetteer, which had been throwing away the region a place string names: San Lorenzo, Puerto Rico had landed in California. [What it cost](/corrections/).

rows.what: The disagreements — fourteen became twelve, and the twelve are sorted
rows.note:
**Two of the fourteen were never disagreements.** An *Antonius* buried at Pula as an infant in 1893 had been matched to the Antonius of Gologorica who died in 1893 aged seventy-nine, because they share a year. Twenty of this archive's burial rows read b = d, a child born and buried in the same year. The anchor test refuses that pairing now and [the correction is logged](/corrections/).

**The twelve that survive are three different problems.**

**Seven are age arithmetic** — death agreed, birth out by one: Josephus, Cattarina, Jacobus, Valentinus, Davide, and Albino and Maria out by two and three. A record that gives an **age** rather than a date produces a birth year that depends on whether the birthday had passed. **Not worth a morning each; worth a sentence on each page.**

**Two are too big for arithmetic**: *Mario De Franceski* 1919 against 1924, and *Girolamo of Omiš* 1632 against 1622.

**Three dispute the death year, and that is the serious kind**: *Clementina Maria* of Gologorica, 1840 here against 1870 — thirty years; *Josephus Lambertus*, same parish, twenty-one; *Lina* of Torrington, two. **[The Gologorica registers](/gologorica-line/) settle two of the three in an afternoon**, and this archive has already read them once.

**Done, 20 September 2026 — each disagreement now says so on the person's own page.** **Fourteen rows annotated, one per disagreement**, matched on **name *and* source** rather than on name alone.

*That distinction cost a first attempt.* Matching on name put the note on **56 rows**, because this roster is record-level and *Maria Defranceschi* alone is twenty-four rows — the annotation would have accused twenty-three innocent namesakes of a disagreement that belongs to one of them. **Stripped and redone.**

**The three kinds are written differently, because they are not the same problem.** The seven off-by-one-to-three births say plainly that *an age produces this* and that the archive keeps its own figure. The two too-big-for-arithmetic say **one side has the wrong man**. The three disputed death years say **this needs the burial register, not a judgement**. And the mirrored *Petrus Defranceschi* pair says what it is: **one man on the roster twice, 1768 and 1765, same death year 1829**, at Gologorica and at Rovinj, standing until somebody resolves them.

rows.what: The four mirrored pairs — one merged, one left standing on purpose
rows.note:
**Maria Defranceschi of Gologorica is merged.** Two rows, born 1786 and 1789, dying the same year at the same parish under two MyHeritage identifiers. Both identifiers are kept on the surviving row; **the birth year is not settled** and the Gologorica baptisms will decide it. [Correction 94](/corrections/).

**Petrus Defranceschi is not merged, and that is the finding.** His two rows disagree on the parish: a Petrus of **Rovinj** resting on a **burial register with an ark**, and a Petrus of **Gologorica** resting on the 2018 family file. Three years and a hundred kilometres apart is either two men or one badly recorded, and **a burial entry outranks a tree entry**. Both rows now carry a note pointing at the other. The Gologorica register decides it, not a merge.

rows.what: The 328 FamilySearch arks — counted and sorted, and waiting on one sign-in
rows.note:
**The list is made and the door is half open.** Of the 405 arks David's own citations name, **328 appear nowhere in this repository**: **234 indexed records** and **94 film images**.

**The session is signed out where it matters.** Tested on 16 September: the waypoint API still answers **200** — which is why [the Međimurje and Pola harvest](/map/) ran this morning — but every route to a record returns **401 Unauthorized**: the persona endpoint, the ark URL itself, and the search service in its place. A waypoint is public; a record is not.

**This archive does not sign in on David's behalf**, so the row is his: sign in to FamilySearch in the in-app browser, and a machine can read all 234 indexed records in one pass at the spacing that has never drawn a throttle.

**The 94 image arks are a different job again** — an image is a page, and a page is read by eye. Those are the ones worth doing first whatever happens: each is a register page David has already looked at.

rows.what: Give the tree back what it does not have — written as a GEDCOM, 494 people
rows.note:
**The file is written: `data/to-the-tree.ged`, 494 people.** It is not an edit to David's tree and it is not going to be one — a GEDCOM is a file he can read before importing and undo after.

**Why 494 and not 780.** The 780 counts roster rows the tree has under no name-and-date match. This file is stricter: it leaves out anybody whose **given names already appear in the tree at all**, even with different dates, because pushing those in makes duplicates rather than fixing anything. 691 were skipped on that test.

**Where they came from**: 168 out of the 2018 family file, 70 from households read off the page, 54 from name indexes, 46 from headstones, 42 from volumes read end to end, 41 from indexed records, 25 from burial registers, 14 from the Gologorica books. **Each carries a NOTE saying which**, 223 carry a FamilySearch ark, and every one links back to its page here.

**No living person is in it.** Twenty were dropped for being flagged living and one more for being born after 1930 with no death recorded — a tree entry is a date by construction, so the rule here is stricter than the name-and-town rule the rest of the site keeps.

rows.what: Ivan's AutoCluster — found, read, and it proves the three Croatian clusters
rows.note:
**It existed all along.** Eight reports came off this account on 15 September and only five were opened; Ivan's was one of the three still unread in the inbox. Found and read on 16 September.

**94 matches in thirteen clusters, and the first holds fifty people** — inside it, David's entire cluster of twelve plus Račić from his cluster of four. From the father those are one cluster, not three.

**Every cluster David has is now decided by arithmetic.** Clusters **2, 5 and 6** have ten, three and two members in his father's report and **none** in his mother's; clusters 1, 3, 4, 7 and 8 are the other way round. **No cluster has members in both.** Cluster 9 is in neither and is still called unplaced.

[The table](/dna/#autoclusters). This morning the Croatian three were an inference from a pool of surnames. **They are proved.**

rows.what: The Senj cluster's ten trees — walked, and the name to chase is Vukelić
rows.note:
**All ten opened on 16 September. They do not name a common couple**, and the reason is that eight of the ten are shallow — three of them show three, seven and twelve people. The two deep ones, at **3,597 people and 1,521**, do not touch each other on a single named person.

**What they share is a surname pool, and one name carries further than the rest: Vukelić stands in three independent trees.** Prpić stands in two. Behind them Blažević, Pavelić, Krmpotić, Tomljanović, Biondić, Lopac, Katalinić, Rončević, Šojat, Butković, Šolić, Delale — every one a Senj-hinterland Bunjevac name.

**So the next name to chase is Vukelić, not Blažević.** Blažević is the one this family carries and therefore the one the eye goes to; Vukelić is the one that recurs across the trees with nothing else in common. [Written up](/dna/#autoclusters).

rows.what: Findmypast transcripts at scale — 424 of them, not ten
rows.note:
The sweep of 16 September read **ten** transcripts out of 424 publishable records, and every one of the ten paid: a Cosulich bride at Cardiff, a GRO volume and page, three Italian sets closed as Neapolitan.

**An index row gives a name and a year. A transcript gives parents, a parish, a ship, a street** — and for the Italian sets, a note in Italian naming the frazione and the grandfather. The transcript pages are fully client-rendered with no server-side payload, so there is no shortcut: they come one navigation at a time, about five seconds each. **Start with the 277 United States passenger records**, whose transcripts name the town of last residence — which is the question this archive actually has: *which of these six hundred are ours?*

---

**21 September — counted, and the order of work is inverted.**

All sixteen pages harvested: **307 records**, and they are **270 passenger and crew lists, 13 naturalisation petitions, 11 Italians to America, 6 Canadian border crossings, 2 Illinois naturalisation index, 2 passport applications, 2 British & Irish Roots, 1 UK outbound**. [The count is on the search register](/searched/).

**The naturalisation petitions carry «Birth place as transcribed» in the transcript itself.** No image, no order, one navigation — and that field *is* the question this item exists to answer. **Thirteen records answer it outright; two hundred and seventy need a plate each.** So the passenger lists are not the place to start.

**All thirteen were read, and all three households were already here** — Joseph at *«Gallignana, Austria»* (the first of the Eleven to go), Peter at *«Basel, Switzerland»*, and Bruno, Gerda and Richard at Brooklyn under the alias *«de Franceschi or Seedorf»*. **That is a real result: the naturalisation route is exhausted and it added nobody.**

**What is left is the 270 passenger records, one plate at a time**, and they should be attacked by *arrival year* rather than alphabetically — the Istrian and Kvarner departures cluster in 1900–1914 and again in 1949–1956.

**Two traps, paid for.** A full page load in this SPA **wipes `window`**, so a harvest must be dumped out of the browser before navigating anywhere — 307 rows were collected and then lost to a single transcript click. And the Apollo cache (`window.__APOLLO_CLIENT__.cache.extract()`) holds **index fields only**: `Record:` keys carry what the results table shows and `FulfillableItem:` carries nothing but a price, **so there is no bulk shortcut to transcripts**. The subscription does cover them — `remainingLegacyCredits` is null and `isPurchased` is true — so nothing is being spent.

---

**Struck, and the reason is that it was already done by a better source.**

The transcripts do carry *Residence* with no image needed — that part of the plan was right. **But [the Ellis Island sweep already read 1,400 arrivals and 429 recorded residences](/searched/), and found exactly two Istrian in the whole database.** Findmypast's 270 are a subset of the same arrivals.

**And there is no query that shortens the job**: `keywordsplace` matches ports, not residence — Domenico's transcript says *«Residence Ponte Alpi»* and searching *«ponte alpi»* returns **zero**, so *«Fiume: 0»* and *«Istria: 0»* are worthless as negatives.

**What survives is narrower and worth doing: the 1949–1956 arrivals**, which the Ellis Island database does not reach, and where the Istrian *esodo* sits. That is a new item, not this one.

rows.what: The Irish, Scottish and English parish collections — opened, and empty but for Cardiff
rows.note:
**One hit in the whole of them.** Of the 44 record sets the surname touches, the only British parish register holding anybody of the name is **Wales Roman Catholic Marriages**, with the single 1876 entry that started all of this. No Irish, Scottish or English parish register has one.

For a Catholic family of the Adriatic that is what one would expect. It is written down so that nobody opens them again. [The register](/searched/).

rows.what: The 1921 Census and the 1939 Register — searched, and nobody of the name is in either
rows.note:
**Nobody.** The sweep paged out every result for four spellings — 644 records, 44 record sets — and neither collection is among them.

**That is a finding.** The *South Wales Echo* called them «an old Cardiff family» in 1896 and a De Franceschi married a Cosulich there in 1876. **By 1921 there is nobody of the name left in England or Wales.** [The register](/searched/).

rows.what: Search Franceschi in Puerto Rico — done, and the thread is closed
rows.note:
**Done, and it ends the question.** Two of the San Lorenzo women were read in full from the 1920 census: *Cármen Colón de Franceschi*, 23, and *Aurora Cruz de Franceschi*, 25. **Both born in Puerto Rico to parents born in Puerto Rico**, both entered as *esposa*, both recorded by the enumerator as **Black**.

An **Afro-Puerto Rican** family two generations on the island by 1920, married into a surname that reached the Caribbean with the nineteenth-century Corsican settlement. **Not immigrants, and not ours.** [Written up](/findmypast/).

rows.what: Cosulich in the newspapers — behind a bot check, so it is David's to run
rows.note:
**The search is right and the door is shut.** Since 16 September this family has a Cosulich in it — [Emerico married Marietta Cosulich at Cardiff on 26 July 1876](/at-sea/) — and the Cosulich were shipowners of Lussinpiccolo and Trieste. **A Cosulich ship at Cardiff in the 1870s, printed beside a De Franceschi master, is the join this archive is missing**, and the shipping columns are where it would be printed.

**Both routes are behind a bot check.** The British Newspaper Archive answers a security challenge before it will show a result; Findmypast's own newspaper search carries a **reCAPTCHA field on the form**. This archive does not work round bot checks, so the search waits for a person.

**What to search, when you have five minutes**: *Cosulich* on its own, then *Cosulich* with **Cardiff**, then *Cosulich* with **Aquilone**. The 153 articles already read under this family's own name are on [the search register](/searched/); the earliest sixty of them are shipping intelligence, which is exactly the column a Cosulich would appear in.

rows.what: The Memphis family — read, named, and pointing at Carnia
rows.note:
**Done.** *Antonio De Franceski*, born **1875 in Italy**, **arrived 1902**, in the 19th Ward of Memphis by 1910 with *Bertha* **born in Germany** and nine children born 1904–1917 — Pietro, Aurora, Alba, Albert, Flora, Estelle, Serena, Juliet, Romeo and a second Anthony. Three censuses, twenty-one records, and **the 1910 sheet spells them «de Franceski»**.

**Born in Italy in 1875 and leaving in 1902 is the Carnian window.** Istria in 1875 was Austria and an American enumerator would have written Austria. It is not proof and the census says no more than «Italy» — **his naturalisation petition would name the town**. [The reading](/findmypast/).

rows.what: Places with no coordinates — four rescued, forty-one named as undrawable
rows.note:
**Done, and the residue is published rather than hidden.** GeoNames files a village too small for its own settlement record under its **church** or its **railway stop**, and this builder was reading only populated places. Reading churches, monasteries, hospitals, stations and localities — and nothing else — put four more on the ground: Mađarevo is a railway stop, Mandalina a halt, Ludina a station, Komarevo a locality.

**A stream or a hill of the same name is not the village and is deliberately left out.** The Glogovnica in the dumps is a river; taking it would have been a wrong dot rather than a missing one.

**Forty-one places carrying 130 volumes still cannot be drawn**, and [the map page now names them](/map/) instead of letting them be invisible. Three are not settlements at all — *Bolnica Dubrovnik*, *Nahodište Dubrovnik* and *Nahodište Split* are a hospital and two foundling houses, and should in the end hang on their towns. **Done, and it found none.** `scripts/living-audit.py` reads the **built HTML** rather than the sources, because the built HTML is the only thing a reader ever sees: **37 people the archive holds as living, against 1,280 pages**, looking for a four-digit year standing in the same run of text as a name.

**Getting to none took three narrowings, and each is a lesson.** The menu lists every page title on every page and one of those titles is a person's name, so the audit reads only what follows the first heading. **No tag may stand between the name and the year** — without that a households row hands the next person's birth year to the one before. And **no sentence may end between them**, because «David Defranceschi. The 1584 plaque…» is prose about a plaque.

What is left is the search index, where the page title *«1948»* sits beside a name in a lowercased string. [On the method page](/method/): a rule enforced at the door should be checked at the window.

rows.what: The naturalisation and passport records — read, and they stop at «Italy»
rows.note:
**The row promised thirteen birthplaces. The transcripts do not carry one.**

Four were read on 16 September — *Giovanni* of Chicago (naturalised 1937), *Giovanni* of Connecticut (passport 1922), *Louis* (passport 1919) and *Tobias de Franceski* (passport 1922). Every one of them gives **«Birth place: Italy»** and nothing finer. Tobias is the exception and only because he was born in the **District of Columbia**.

**The town is on the image, not in the index.** Findmypast holds the images and links them from each transcript, and the transcripts carry the NARA reference that would fetch the same page from Washington — *M1490 roll 1807*, *roll 1008*, *roll 1842*, *M1285 roll 41*.

So the work is a different job from the one written down: **eighteen images to read by eye**, not eighteen transcripts to harvest. Two are [already an errand](/errands/) because a petition is worth ordering whether or not the image reads.

*Corrected the same day it was written, which is the right speed for a wrong plan.*

---

**21 September 2026 — the images are open, and two towns are out.**

**The viewer was never the obstacle.** A Findmypast transcript id for these sets *is* a FamilySearch film and frame — `US_PASSPORT_APPLICATIONS/**007572652**/**00658**/…` — so the plate can be fetched directly and read on a canvas, with no viewer, no filmstrip and no paging. [The route is written down](/searched/).

**Louis De Franceschi was born at Sequals, Province of Udine, on 3 November 1873**; father **Pietro**, dead by 1919; Havre to Washington in February 1907; naturalised 4 October 1915; **cement decorator**, which is the Sequals trade. **Giovanni DeFranceschi was born at Castronovo on 10 December 1876**; father **Francesco**, dead by 1922; Havre to Torrington, Connecticut in April 1903; naturalised at Winsted in 1911.

**And the index was never wrong.** The form asks the father's birthplace in one blank labelled *«(Country.)»*, so *«Italy»* is the whole of that field. The town lives on the applicant's own line, and only on the **naturalized-citizen** form — which is why **Tobias's native-citizen application of 1922 has no town to give, and his father's has Sequals**.

**Still to read: the remaining images**, and the **Chicago naturalisation of 1937**, which is a different series with a different image path.

rows.what: Search the Hungarian and German record sets under the Hungarian and German forms of the given names
rows.note:
**Every sweep this archive has run searched the SURNAME.** Nine spellings of it, systematically — *Defranceschi, De Franceschi, Defranceski, De Franceski, Defrančeski, Defranzeschi, Franceschi*, and the two Australian manglings *Zorafko* and *Zdrafko*. That is why the Australian and Arolsen files were found.

**The given name has never been varied once.** Out of 312 rows in the [research log](/research-log/), eight mention searching by a forename and all eight are a hunt for one named person, not a sweep.

**That is a hole with a shape.** Fiume was a *corpus separatum* of the Crown of St Stephen and its civil registration went over to **Hungarian in 1895**: a clerk there wrote **János**, not Giovanni, **József**, not Giuseppe, **Péter**, not Pietro. [Hungaricana](/method/) is free and this archive already uses it. The same for the Austrian sets and **Johann, Josef, Franz, Andreas**. Sixteen Hungarian forms are already sitting in the records here, unrecognised until today — and they got in by accident, not by being looked for. [The seven columns](/your-name/) are a search plan that has never been run.

---

**Run on 20 September, and the answer is a clean methodological finding: for this name the Magyarised forename is a dead end, but the Magyarised word order is not.**

Sixteen Hungarian forms were put to Hungaricana as phrases, surname first as Hungarian requires. **Fourteen returned nothing at all** — *Gyula* (Julius), *Antal* (Anton), *János* (Ivan/Johann), *Bálint* (Valentin), *Vincze*, *Károly*, *Mihály*, *József*, *Miklós*, *Alajos* (Alois), *Tódor* (Theodor), *Lajos*, *István*, *Ede* (Eduard).

**Two returned, and the pair explains the other fourteen.** *«Defranceschi **Ferencz**»* gives **4 hits** — the Fiume harbour master's pension, his orphan Francziska's grace allowance twice over, and a **Budapest directory of 1848**. *«Defranceschi **Péter**»* gives **1**. The rule behind it: the Hungarian state printed its *sentences* in Hungarian and its *service lists* in German, so the surname inverts but the forename mostly does not. **Ferencz is the exception because it is a spelling, not a translation** — Hungarian *cz* for German *z* in Franz.

**The control matters more than the zeros.** Fourteen nils would mean nothing if the method could not produce a hit; *Ferencz* returning four known records is what makes the nils evidence. The sweep was run because [the search log](/research-log/) showed 312 rows in which the surname had been varied nine ways and **the forename never once**.

**And it was not empty.** *Péter* turned up **a fourteenth man for [the imperial roll](/imperial/)** — *«beim Husz. Reg. Nr 8 · Defranceschi Peter Dr · beim Garnisons-Spitale»*, **Militärschematismus 1867**, a regimental physician and the second doctor on a roll that had one.

rows.what: Where a Cardiff crew agreement of 1876–77 actually is — answered: three places, and the ship's number is the key to all three
rows.note:
**Two things are now settled and the third is the whole job.**

**Settled: the crew lists are catalogued to the person, and further back than expected.** *«Ship: Belgravian; Official number: 98611. William G S Nash; rank/rating, Master; age, 57; place of birth…»* — and not only in the 1915 series: **BT 99/1302/37 is 1881** and **BT 99/1718/16B is 1891**, both with name, rating, age and birthplace. This archive's first explanation of the blank — that shipping is catalogued by vessel and year rather than by master — was simply wrong, and is [retracted](/research-log/).

**Settled: the name is not in it.** *Franceschi rank rating* **0**, *Defranceschi seaman* **0**, against **827** for *«place of birth, Italy» master*. The index is dense, so the absence means something.

**Open: Kew holds only a fraction of the nineteenth-century agreements** — the bulk went to the **Maritime History Archive at Memorial University, Newfoundland**. **Emerico married at Cardiff in Q3 1876 and the *Aquilone* cleared the Bute Docks for Guadaloupe on 11 December 1877.** Establish which repository holds Cardiff-registered agreements for those two years, and write to whichever it is.

---

**Answered on 20 September from Kew's own catalogue, and the question had the wrong shape.** It is not *«Kew or Newfoundland»*. It is **three repositories and one number.**

· **The National Archives, BT 99** — its series description says it plainly: *«a **ten per cent sample** of agreements and crew lists (with log-books where they survive) for the years 1861-1938»*.
· **Maritime History Archive, Memorial University of Newfoundland** — catalogued in Discovery as an external holding: *«Registrar General of Shipping and Seamen, crew lists, agreements and official logbooks (**c70% of total**)», 1863-1938*.
· **County record offices in the British Isles** hold the rest — for a Cardiff-registered ship that means **Glamorgan Archives**.

**And the finding aid that resolves which:** **MF17** at Kew, *«Index to location of crew agreements and logbooks of vessels (microfiche)», 1863-1913* — produced, pointedly, **by the Maritime History Archive itself**. Its entries are *«arranged according to the **official number** of the vessel, the vessels are not named»*.

**So the chain is fixed and its first link is missing.** Ship's name → **Official Number** (from the *Mercantile Navy List*) → MF17 → the repository → the agreement, which names master, crew, ages and birthplaces. **Every BT 99 piece in the catalogue is titled by official numbers alone**, which is why searching the surname returns nothing and always will: the index is of ships, not men.

**Which makes [the Cardiff marriage certificate](/errands/) the hinge of the whole maritime thread.** GRO Cardiff, Q3 1876, vol. 11A p. 428. If Emerico's occupation is given as master mariner, and better still if a vessel is named, the Official Number follows from the *Mercantile Navy List* and MF17 says where to write. Without a ship's name there is nothing to look up, in any of the three places.

rows.what: The rest of the British record: 1861–1911 censuses and the GRO for the Cardiff household
rows.note:
**«An old Cardiff family»** is a phrase a newspaper used in 1896 and this archive has never tested against a census. Findmypast's 1921 Census and 1939 Register [hold nobody of the name](/findmypast/), which dates the disappearance but not the family. **The censuses between Emerico's marriage in 1876 and 1911 have not been searched at all** — and the subscription that would do it is already paid for. Kew is not the place for this; the GRO and the census are.

---

**21 September 2026 — searched, and the answer is the other surname.**

**No person of this name, in any spelling, is enumerated anywhere in Glamorgan in any census from 1841 to 1921.** *Defranceschi* and *De Franceschi* return **nothing** across Great Britain for births 1815–1895; the wildcard *Defrance\** returns **no census record at all** in Glamorgan; and the one historic Cardiff hit on *Franceschi\** is a **Franceschini**, a different name.

**The Cosulich are there the whole time** — Swansea 1871, St John Cardiff 1881 and 1891, Barry 1921, Rhyl 1939. **«An old Cardiff family» is the bride's family, not the groom's.** [The reading is on the search register](/searched/) and the household is [set out under Cosulich](/married-in/).

**What is left is the GRO, and it is an order, not a search**: the 1876 marriage certificate (Cardiff Q3 1876, 11A/428) for Emerico's occupation, and the Cardiff birth index of the late 1870s for the daughter who played at the 1896 Exhibition.

rows.what: Read the Crikvenica marriage film end to end — the only Vinodol marriage register on film that reaches 1885–1908
rows.note:
**Begun 17 September 2026, and the survey of the shelf came first because it changed the target.**

**Across the whole Vinodol, one marriage register on film reaches the years wanted.** Ledenice's *Vjenčani* stops at **1882**; Novi Vinodolski's at **1859**; Bribir's at **1858**; Grižane has no marriage film at all. Only **Crikvenica, Vjenčani 1859–1908**, covers 1885–1890 and 1908. If the marriage of **Josip Defranceschi × Anna Kalanj** is on free film anywhere, it is in that one volume — and if it is not in it, the answer is a letter to the parish office at Ledenice or Novi, not another search.

**The film is open and mapped.** 272 images, DGS **2084742**; every image's ark captured from the waypoint API and held in the session scratchpad; full-resolution pages (about 6000 × 4150) reachable directly, and legible. Year anchors read off the pages themselves: **image 61 = 1862 · image 161 = «Godina 1890» · image 200 = 1897**, so 1885–1890 falls at about **images 138–165** and 1908 at the end of the book.

**The honest cost of «end to end».** The archive's own standard is that a volume is not marked read until every page has been looked at. A page is a two-page spread of about four marriages, and the browser returns 800 pixels at a time, so a spread needs three or four looks. **272 images is therefore something like nine hundred reads** — an afternoon, not a minute, and it is the price of being able to put a green mark on that volume and mean it.

---

**20 September: 17 of 272 read, and three consecutive years are now closed end to end.**

**1887, 1888 and 1889 are complete** — images 151–160, entries 1–19, 1–19 and 1–13, with the priest's own closing line on each: *«U Crikvenici dne 31 prosinca 1889. Alexander Car, župnik.»* **Not one Defranceschi in any of them**, in the couple columns or the parents' and witnesses' columns.

**Why those three years and not others.** Anton Rudolf was born at **Klenovica on 20 January 1890**, so his parents **Josip Defranceschi and Anna Kalanj** married before that; **Ledenice marriages stop in 1882**, which leaves Crikvenica as the only Vinodol marriage register on film covering the window. **1887–1889 is the heart of it, and they are not in it.** That does not close the question — 1883–1886 and the first weeks of 1890 are still unread, and they may have married in Klenovica's or Novi's own parish rather than the bride's — but it removes the likeliest three years.

**One gap to go back for:** **1888 entries 16 and 17** fall between images 157 and 158 and have not been seen. The year is otherwise complete.

**The scratchpad was wiped between sessions and had to be rebuilt** — all 272 arks re-derived from the waypoint and **verified against the previous session's record** (image 156 must be `3QS7-899X-R4S`, and it is). `METHOD.md` now carries the rebuild recipe so the next wipe costs minutes.

**The reading method changed and is much better.** The old auto-crop locked onto the film frame rather than the page, because this film's grey base is as bright as the paper. It is replaced by a **fixed left/right split** — each half of the frame drawn into 800×1100 — which doubles the effective resolution and made the hands legible. Two screenshots per image; about 255 images to go.

**And one question for David, which is a scope question rather than a reading one.** The witness column of 1888 no. 18 carries **«Frančić»**. The declared in-scope list at [/name/#scope](/name/#scope) includes **«Franceschich»**, which is the Italianised spelling of exactly that Croatian patronymic of *Franjo*. **Either Frančić is in scope and this film has hits, or Franceschich should not be on the in-scope list.** It cannot be both. *Flagged, not decided.*

---

**20 September, second sitting: 1883 is complete, and a year label had to be corrected before it did any harm.**

**The correction first.** Image 132 was logged an hour earlier as *«Godina 1885»*. Read at full magnification it is unmistakably **«Godine 1883»** — the same flourished hand that had already turned 1888 into 1877 at low resolution. **The digit was re-read, not guessed**, and everything then fell into place: 1882 closes on image 131 with *«Crikvenica dne 31 prosinca 1882»*, so the next year must be 1883. **1883–1886 is images 132–150**, which is four years across nineteen images — the same four or five images a year as the rest of the film.

**1883 is now read end to end: images 132–136, entries 1 to 23, and no Defranceschi.** The year closes with blank ruled rows after entry 23, which is how this register ends a year. The names are the same closed village as ever — Car, Kalnić, Škiljan, Kristofor, Vračić, Bernjac, Škomerža, Kulentić, Matejčić, Manestar — with two outsiders worth noting: **no. 19, Josip Car, a clerk at the royal district tax office at Karlovac**, and **no. 21, Ivan Barac of Grižane marrying Ana Car of Crikvenica**.

**1881 and 1882 were read on the way past** (images 124–131) and are also clean, which was not asked for but costs nothing to keep.

**Read so far: 31 images of 272**, and **1883, 1887, 1888 and 1889 are complete years**. Still to do for David's window: **1884, 1885 and 1886 — images 137 to 150**.

*Method note: the crop is now a magnified window on the left page rather than a whole-frame view, because the couple columns are what carry the surname. The parents' and witnesses' columns on the right page are a second pass, still owed for 1883.*

---

**1883 to 1889 is now read end to end — seven consecutive years, 144 marriages, and not one Defranceschi.**

| year | images | marriages |
|---|---|---|
| 1883 | 132–136 | 23 |
| 1884 | 137–141 | 25 |
| 1885 | 142–148 | 31 |
| 1886 | 148–150 | 14 |
| 1887 | 151–154 | 19 |
| 1888 | 155–158 | 19 |
| 1889 | 158–160 | 13 |

Each year closes in the priest's own hand — *«U Crikvenici dne 31 prosinca 1886»*, and so on — so these are **whole years, not samples**. 1881 and 1882 were read on the way in and are clean too.

**What that settles.** Anton Rudolf was born at **Klenovica on 20 January 1890**; his parents **Josip Defranceschi and Anna Kalanj** must therefore have married by 1889. **Ledenice marriages stop in 1882.** Crikvenica was the one Vinodol marriage register on film that covered the gap, and **the seven years that matter are now read and they are not in it.**

**So the marriage is not at Crikvenica, and the search moves to three named places**: the parish that actually served **Klenovica** — Novi Vinodolski — whose register is the obvious next order; **Ledenice after 1882**, whose later volumes are not on this film and must be asked for from the Matični ured; and **Bribir or Grižane**, the two neighbouring parishes whose people marry into Crikvenica on these very pages. *This is a redirection built on a complete reading, not on a sample.*

**The village these pages describe is worth recording for its own sake.** Ninety-three marriages in four years among **Car, Kalnić, Škiljan, Kristofor, Vračić, Bernjac, Kovrić, Jurinčić, Veljačić, Matejčić, Manestar, Brozičević, Župan** — marrying each other, house number after house number. The outsiders are countable on one hand and each one is an occupation: **Mirko Car, master mariner** (1885 no. 24); **Adalberto Radil, a baker** (1885 no. 26); **Ivan Vinko Grohovac, temporary schoolmaster** from Grohovo by Rijeka (1886 no. 4); **Eduardo Janić of Bakar** (1886 no. 7); **Josip Car, clerk at the royal tax office at Karlovac** (1883 no. 19); and **Marija-Eva Pilz of Gospić** (1886 no. 10), the only German name in four years. **A Defranceschi would have stood out exactly as these do** — which is why the negative can be trusted.

**Read so far: 45 of 272 images.** The declared strength for 1883–1886 is **the couple columns on every page** — both surnames, occupation, house number — plus the parents' and witnesses' columns on image 150. **The parents' and witnesses' columns for the rest of 1883–1889 are a second pass and are still owed**; a Defranceschi could in principle stand there as a father or a witness without appearing as a bride or groom.

**The last three pages are not entries at all, and they are worth having.** Images 269–271 are blank ruled pages with **loose certificates pasted onto them** — the parish's own working papers, kept in the back of the book:

- a **freedom-to-marry certificate of 16 November 1868** for a Tomas Škrolin-Lončar of Crikvenica, signed **Josip Medvedić, crikvenički vikar**;

**What is left.** The first half — **images 4 to 123, the years 1859 to 1882.** Those years matter less for Josip and Anna, who cannot have married before about 1883, but they are the years in which **a Defranceschi grandfather could have come and gone**, and the standard for marking this volume read is every page. ## The two Italian families of Crikvenica turn up as witnesses — and that is the sharpest form this negative has taken.

**1870 complete at 25 marriages; 1871 read to entry 11. Images 4–76 done.**

On **10 January 1871** the witnesses to a Crikvenica wedding are, in the priest's own words and confirmed at magnification: **«Emericus Benedetti, mercator in loco, & Eugenius Montanari».**

Both names have been met before in this reading, and both arrived from outside:

- **Montanari** first appears in **1865**, when a Maria-Anna Montanari marries the clerk of the Vinodol district court;
- **Benedetti** in **1868**, when Antonius Benedetti of **Fiume**, a merchant, marries a Slovene bride from Carniola.

**By 1871 they are no longer passing through.** Benedetti is *mercator **in loco*** — the merchant *of this place* — and the two of them stand together at a village wedding, which is what settled families do. The register names them, gives their trade, and states their residence.

**This is the strongest form the argument can take in the first half of the book.** Crikvenica in the 1860s did receive Italian-named incomers; it kept them; it wrote them into the register as grooms, as brides, and as witnesses, with occupations attached. **The parish had both the vocabulary and the occasion. Across 1859–1871 it never once had cause to write Defranceschi.**

*Also on these pages: 1870 no. 16, magnified — **Dominus Vitus Lenčić, localis scholae magister**, of **Lokve**, marrying Maria Magdalena Planinz. The village schoolmaster, another outsider with a profession, another name written down in full.*

**A third bishop signs the book — and this one is the earliest.**

Image 79, across the foot of the 1871 spread: *«Praesentes Copulatorum Matriculas … Nos in Crikvenica occasione Nostrae Canonicae Visitationis revidimus et approbavimus. Sic in Crikvenica die 13ª Octobris 1871.»* — **Venceslaus Soić, Episcopus Segniensis et Modrusiensis**.

That makes **three episcopal visitations** caught in this reading of one volume: **Soić in 1871**, **Posilović in 1891**, **Maurović in 1899**.
